claims.text: Hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10 with multilevel chemical fluctuations has previously been synthesized.
A physics-informed, multi-fidelity machine-learning framework can accurately predict the mechanical properties of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework can reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to first-principles and CALPHAD approaches.
Coarse-grained descriptors can capture the mesoscale domain architecture of the hierarchical alloy.
Coarse-grained descriptors can capture the alloy's nanoscale chemical fluctuations.
Physics-based constraints narrow the parameter space relevant to mechanical-property prediction.
Physics-based constraints guide the machine-learning model toward mechanically relevant predictions.
Combining coarse-grained approximations with selected high-fidelity simulations bridges relevant length scales.
Multi-fidelity training enables rapid surrogate predictions.
The combined framework can replicate mechanical behavior observed in expensive full-scale simulations and experiments.
The framework will predict Young's modulus within 10% of experimental values.
The framework will predict yield strength within 10% of experimental values.
The framework will predict fracture toughness within 20% of experimental values.
The framework will reduce computational time by approximately tenfold relative to conventional methods.
High-fidelity ab initio, CALPHAD, and full-scale first-principles methods are computationally intensive for this prediction problem.
Conventional methods are particularly inefficient for predicting complex fracture properties.
The framework may become unreliable when microstructural features deviate significantly from the training range.
The framework may become unreliable at temperatures or strain rates outside its calibrated range.
Previously unmodeled scales of chemical disorder may dominate mechanical behavior and invalidate the framework.
The proposed accuracy and efficiency estimates are provisionally extrapolated from analogous studies.
